title: The Middle-Length, closed
hookLine: from the root of all things to the training of the senses

lines: THE FIRST: THE MONKS WERE NOT PLEASED.
THE LAST: EYES THAT STAY OPEN.
A HUNDRED AND FIFTY IN BETWEEN.
cards: The first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings ends on a strange note. The text says the monks did not delight in what the Buddha had said about the root of all things. It doesn't say why.
The last discourse ends with a young brahmin sitting silent and a quiet teaching about eyes that stay open. In between, a hundred and fifty more.

teach.b: The Pali name is Majjhima Nikaya: the middle collection. Middle here means middle-length, not as long as the long discourses, not as short as the connected ones.
It's arranged in three groups of fifty, the root fifty, the middle fifty and the last fifty, and the last group has two extra, which is how you get a hundred and fifty-two. Here's the road we walked.

teach.h: FROM THE ROOT TO THE SENSES
teach.b: The root of all things, and all the taints. Heirs in dhamma, not in things. Fear met in the forest at night.
The stained cloth that won't take the dye. The saw, and goodwill even under it. The water snake and the raft.
Relay chariots. The noble search. Milk and water.
Saccaka sweating. Examine even the teacher. Rahula and the mirror, then the earth.
Angulimala, read whole. Any wood makes fire. Breathing in sixteen steps.
A hall empty of elephants. One fine night. Punna going west.
Rahula freed under a tree, six sets of six, and finally, seeing without being swept. Now the small surprise in the name.

teach.h: THE SAME WORD AS THE MIDDLE WAY
teach.b: Majjhima is the same word as the middle in the middle way, majjhima patipada, the path between indulgence and self-torment that the Buddha named in his first teaching. The title is about length, not doctrine.
But the collection keeps showing that path anyway: not grabbing, not pushing away, not shutting the eyes, not drowning in what they see.
A hundred and fifty-two ways of walking down the middle.

how: The Majjhima Nikaya is one of the five collections of the Sutta Pitaka in the Pali Canon, studied and recited in Theravada monasteries; many of its discourses have parallels in the Chinese Madhyama Agama, preserved by another early school.

o: the teaching of the middle way itself
the middle stage of a monk's training

games.q: the Middle-Length, closed: tap the pairs.
p: plus two: a hundred and fifty-two

s: the collection is called middle because it teaches the middle way
the name refers to length: middle-length discourses. it's the same word, though.
the first discourse ends with the monks not pleased
the text says they did not delight in his words, and doesn't say why.
the collection is arranged in three groups of about fifty
the root fifty, the middle fifty and the last fifty, which has fifty-two.

games.q: you've finished all hundred and fifty-two discourses. what does tomorrow bring?
games.why: tomorrow opens the Digha Nikaya, thirty-four long discourses, many told as stories and conversations.

practice: Let one line from the whole collection come, whichever arrives: the raft is for crossing, all of it changing, empty of this, see and stay.
Say it once, quietly, and let it go silent; when the mind wanders, bring back just the line, then the quiet, not grabbing it, not pushing it away.

wordCard.voice: The Middle-Length. The Majjhima Nikaya, a hundred and fifty-two discourses, from the root of all things to the training of the senses.

orig.note: Pali majjhima: middle. Majjhima Nikaya, the middle-length collection; majjhima patipada, the middle way.

carryVoice: Your line: the middle way, in words. The shelf is closed; the path it kept showing is still open. That's day five hundred twenty-one.
